name: Pikes Peak
generated_description:
Pikes Peak is a 14,114-foot summit in Colorado. With roughly 5,518 feet of topographic prominence, it stands well above the surrounding terrain. The Barr Trail covers 11.1 miles with about 7,375 feet of elevation gain — a steady climb. It's rated Strenuous overall.

The Route

The climbing is spread fairly evenly from start to finish rather than stacked into one steep section. The steepest stretch arrives around mile 10.29, gaining roughly 900 feet per mile — expect a slow, deliberate pace through here. From the trailhead at about 6,706 feet, the route tops out near 14,081 feet. You'll cross above treeline on the way up, so the upper route is exposed to weather — check the forecast and turn around if conditions build.

Getting There

The trailhead is at 38.85578, -104.93389 (tap for driving directions). It's roughly 5 miles west of Colorado Springs, Colorado. Arrive early on weekends — trailhead lots at popular peaks fill quickly, and cell service is often unreliable once you leave the highway.

When to Go

The reliable snow-free window is roughly July through September. At this elevation, afternoon thunderstorms are a serious summer hazard — start early and plan to be off the upper mountain by midday. Outside that window expect snow travel and bring traction and navigation skills to match.

Know Before You Go

The Strenuous rating comes from the National Park Service difficulty formula, which weighs total distance against elevation gain. Most hikers should budget about 7.5 hours of moving time; add margin for breaks, photos and the descent. Download the GPX track from this page before you go — cell coverage is unreliable in the mountains and a saved route works offline in any GPS app. Conditions change: verify current access, closures and weather with the official land manager before you go. Trail data is sourced from OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL).

Looking to link objectives or plan a weekend? Nearby summits include Mount Blue Sky, Mount Princeton and Mount Antero — each has its own guide on this site.

faqs.question: How long does it take to hike Pikes Peak?
faqs.answer: The Barr Trail is 11.1 miles with about 7,375 feet of elevation gain, and most hikers take roughly 7.5 hours of moving time. Add time for breaks and conditions — winter or wet weather can double the trip.

faqs.question: How hard is the Pikes Peak hike?
faqs.answer: It's rated Strenuous using the National Park Service difficulty formula (11.1 miles, 7,375 ft of gain — about 650 ft of climbing per mile). The elevation profile on this page shows exactly where the steep sections fall.

faqs.question: Where is the Pikes Peak trailhead?
faqs.answer: The trailhead is at 38.85578, -104.93389 in Colorado. Use the driving-directions link in the Getting There section above, and note that parking at popular trailheads fills early on weekends.

faqs.question: Are dogs allowed on the Pikes Peak trail?
faqs.answer: Rules vary by land manager — national parks often prohibit dogs on trails, while most national forests allow them on leash. Check with the managing agency for this trail before bringing your dog, and pack out waste.

faqs.question: When is the best time to hike Pikes Peak?
faqs.answer: July through September is the reliable snow-free window. Start early to avoid afternoon thunderstorms above treeline.

faqs.question: How tall is Pikes Peak?
faqs.answer: Pikes Peak stands at 14,114 feet (4,302 meters) in Colorado.
